titleText.noteEn: The official English title text drops the h sounds in 'ardly and 'er, making the end of supercollider sound like “collide 'er” and invoking the stock “I hardly know her” joke; its two spaces after the question mark are preserved exactly. The Spanish archive keeps the flirtatious formula with la even though supercolisionador is grammatically masculine, so it is a deliberately nonliteral and grammatically playful adaptation rather than a direct Spanish pun.

regions.labelEs: OYE, EL LHC SE ENCIENDE HOY. ESTA PODRÍA SER NUESTRA ÚLTIMA NOCHE EN LA TIERRA.

excludedUnits.rationale: LHC is the international English-derived acronym for the Large Hadron Collider, not a Spanish lexical word occurrence.

applications.explanationEn: Oye is the familiar singular command form of oír, used here to get the listener's attention.
Esta names one situation as the subject, so podría expresses what that situation could or might be rather than what the speaker could do.
Podría carries the imagined possibility, while ser remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: NO FASTIDIES. NI SIQUIERA HAN EMPEZADO CON LAS COLISIONES, Y NO HARÁN NADA QUE NO HAYAN HECHO YA LOS RAYOS CÓSMICOS.

applications.explanationEn: No comes before fastidies, the special negative-command form used to address one familiar listener.
The two-word exclamation reacts with dismissive disbelief rather than making a literal request about one specific annoyance.
Ni and siquiera combine to rule out even the minimal stage being discussed.
Han is the helper form for the implied plural subject, and empezado is the unchanged completed-action form.
Hacer uses its irregular future stem har- plus the plural ending -án.

applications.exampleEs: NO HARÁN NADA QUE NO HAYAN
applications.explanationEn: No harán nada denies that any qualifying action exists, so que is followed by the special form hayan. The second no belongs inside the description but is not what creates the negated antecedent.
Hayan is the plural special form of haber required by the denied description, and hecho is hacer's unchanged completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: EH, NO HE DICHO QUE NO.

applications.explanationEn: He is the first-person helper form, and dicho is decir's irregular completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: SOY ESTUDIANTE DE POSGRADO DE FÍSICA. NECESITO UNA EXCUSA PARA IR DE MARCHA.

applications.explanationEn: Para introduces the purpose, and ir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Ir is the unchanged form required after para, while de marcha supplies the fixed partying meaning.

regions.labelEs: ¿ENTONCES TE APUNTAS A UNA NOCHE A FONDO CON UN EXTRAÑO ENCANTADOR?

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the familiar listener, apuntas is the matching verb form, and a introduces una noche as the proposed plan.
The fixed two-word expression adds the idea of full intensity.
Extraño functions as the person noun here, and the neutral descriptive adjective encantador follows it.
Encantador uses its masculine singular form because it describes un extraño, a masculine singular person noun.

regions.labelEs: EH, NI SIQUIERA TE HE INVITADO A UNA COPA.

applications.explanationEn: Ni siquiera emphasizes that even this expected preliminary step has not occurred.
He is the first-person helper form, and invitado is the unchanged completed-action form.

applications.exampleEs: TE HE INVITADO A UNA COPA
applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the invited person, invitado supplies the invitation verb, and a introduces una copa as what is offered. He belongs to the separate completed-action construction.
Hasta sets an endpoint and arriba makes that endpoint the top, expressing complete fullness.

cards.noteEn: Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; presents the thing as changing
cards.noteEn: With verbs such as reducir and ampliar, se lets Spanish describe a change without naming anyone who causes it. English often uses a simple verb such as “shrinks” or “widens.”
Enciende is the present form of encender for one person or thing. With se, encenderse describes a device or system starting up without naming whoever activates it.

cards.answerEn: Natural cosmic rays already produce very energetic particle collisions, a comparison used to argue that starting the Large Hadron Collider would not create a new planet-destroying danger.
cards.noteEn: The opening fear imagines the collider's startup ending life on Earth. The reply invokes cosmic rays, which have struck Earth naturally for an extremely long time, and the physics student treats the alleged catastrophe mostly as an excuse for a party. That contrast supplies the scientific setup for the joke.

Podría is a form of poder used for an imagined possibility. To make this form, poder changes to podr- and adds -ía. The same written form can mean “I could” or can go with one other person or thing; the stated subject shows which meaning applies.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.promptEs: orden negativa de tú: no + verbo
cards.questionEn: How do you tell one friend or familiar person not to do something?
cards.answerEn: Put no before the verb's special negative-command form. If the verb uses te, put te between no and the verb.
cards.noteEn: For a regular -ar verb, the negative form usually ends in -es: hablar becomes no hables. Regular -er and -ir verbs usually end in -as: comer becomes no comas. A short word such as te goes before this negative form, as in no te levantes.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “come on!” or “give me a break!” informally when something sounds unbelievable or annoying?
cards.answerEn: Use ¡No fastidies! as an informal exclamation of disbelief, protest, or annoyance.
cards.noteEn: The words literally form a negative command from fastidiar, “to bother or annoy.” As a fixed reaction, however, the expression often challenges what was just said rather than asking someone to stop a specific act. It is informal and can sound sharper than a neutral response.

example.es: ¡No fastidies! Eso no puede ser verdad.
example.en: Come on! That cannot be true.

cards.noteEn: Fastidies is the special form of fastidiar used after no to tell one familiar person not to bother or annoy someone. The complete exclamation no fastidies also has a common idiomatic use taught separately.

cards.answerEn: not even (as part of ni siquiera)
cards.noteEn: Ni begins the fixed emphasis ni siquiera, which says that even a minimal or surprising possibility does not apply.

cards.questionEn: How do you emphasize that not even a minimal or surprising possibility applies?
cards.answerEn: Use ni siquiera before the excluded thing or action.
cards.noteEn: Ni siquiera means ‘not even.’ Before a verb, it can supply negation by itself. When it appears later, Spanish commonly also uses no before the verb.

example.en: He did not even open the message.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes ni siquiera, ‘not even’
cards.noteEn: Siquiera completes ni siquiera. Learn the two words together for the common meaning ‘not even.’

example.es: No tengo ni siquiera un minuto.
example.en: I do not even have one minute.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Empezado is the completed-action form of empezar, “to start.” It follows a form of haber in expressions such as han empezado, “they have started.”

cards.questionEn: Which verb form follows que when you deny that a person or thing exists or has the described property?
cards.answerEn: Use the special subjunctive form after que because the description is being denied, not stated as a fact.
cards.noteEn: An antecedent is the person or thing described by que; a negated antecedent is one the wording presents as absent or not fitting. The special verb form is called the subjunctive. Compare the ordinary statement vive in Conozco a alguien que vive aquí with viva in No conozco a nadie que viva aquí. The plus signs in the prompt mean “followed by.”

example.es: No conozco a nadie que viva aquí.
example.en: I do not know anyone who lives here.

cards.answerEn: they will do; they will make
cards.noteEn: Harán is the future form of hacer used with ellos or ellas. The same form can also mean “you all will do” with ustedes when the listeners are the subject.

example.en: They will do the work tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.
After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.
Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to a completed action when the surrounding sentence treats it as uncertain, denied, desired, or otherwise not simply stated as fact?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching special form of haber—haya, hayas, hayamos, hayáis, or hayan—then the action verb's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These special haber forms belong to what is called the subjunctive, used when a clause is framed through uncertainty, denial, wishes, or similar attitudes rather than asserted directly. The completed-action form, called the past participle, stays unchanged: haya hablado, hayas comido, hayan vivido. Only haber changes for the person or group.

example.es: No conozco a nadie que haya visitado Perú.
example.en: I do not know anyone who has visited Peru.

cards.noteEn: Hecho is the irregular completed-action form of hacer, “to do” or “to make.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “done.”

example.en: I have already done the homework.

cards.noteEn: A rayo can be a ray or beam of radiation, a lightning bolt, or a sudden streak. The scientific labels here use the radiation sense.

example.en: The rays pass through the material.

cards.noteEn: Cósmico describes something related to the cosmos or outer space. The ending changes to match the noun.
Dicho is the irregular completed-action form of decir, “to say.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “said.”
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Estudiante can refer to a male or female student; the surrounding article or other context can show gender when it matters.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
A posgrado is advanced study pursued after completing an initial university degree.

example.en: She is doing graduate studies in history.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to go; to work or run
cards.noteEn: Ir normally means “to go.” In ir bien or ir mal, it describes how something works or is going: va bien means “it works” or “it’s going well.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone goes out partying?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of ir, then de marcha.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes for the person and time: voy, vas, vamos, fueron, and so on. De marcha stays together and refers to going out for lively nightlife or partying, not to marching somewhere.

example.en: We are going out partying on Saturday.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links ir to marcha in ir de marcha
cards.noteEn: The de is required in the fixed expression ir de marcha, which means to go out partying. Translating de by itself would hide how the expression works.

example.en: We are going out partying on Friday.

cards.noteEn: In the fixed expression ir de marcha, marcha refers to lively nightlife or partying rather than a literal march or movement.

example.en: They went out partying last night.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “you” verb used with te
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs use te when the person affected is the informal listener. The meaning belongs to the whole verb pattern, so English may not translate te separately.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone signs up for, joins, or is willing to take part in a plan?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun and form of apuntarse, then a and the plan or activity.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun changes with the person: me apunto, te apuntas, se apunta, nos apuntamos. The a introduces what that person joins. The plus sign in the prompt means “followed by,” and the rest of the prompt names the plan or activity that fills that slot.

cards.answerEn: are you joining; are you up for it (with te and a)
cards.noteEn: Apuntas is the present tú form of apuntar. In te apuntas a, the full verb apuntarse means to sign up, join in, or be willing to take part.

cards.answerEn: to; for (required after apuntarse before the activity)
cards.noteEn: Apuntarse uses a before the plan, event, or activity someone joins or is willing to do.

example.en: I am in for the dinner.

cards.promptEs: encima o abajo · una copa · hasta arriba
cards.answerEn: The flirtation turns a question about being on top or below into sexual-position innuendo, then echoes the vertical wording in an order for drinks filled to the top.
cards.noteEn: The joke escalates unusually quickly from an invitation to a positional question. The response retreats to the convention of first buying someone a drink, but the final order keeps the above-and-below vocabulary active. The Spanish adaptation uses margaritas and hasta arriba, so its closing wordplay differs from the official English whiskey-sour wording.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a fondo, “thoroughly” or “all-out”
cards.noteEn: The a combines with fondo to form the fixed expression a fondo. Learn the two words together rather than translating this a on its own.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is done thoroughly, fully, or all-out?
cards.answerEn: Use a fondo to describe going to the fullest extent or depth.
cards.noteEn: Fondo literally suggests a bottom or depth. In this fixed expression, that image conveys thoroughness or full intensity. The exact English wording changes with what is being described: study a subject thoroughly, clean deeply, or go all-out.
Fondo can mean a bottom or depth. In the fixed expression a fondo, that image becomes the idea of doing something thoroughly, fully, or all-out.
With an article and no following noun, extraño can itself name a male stranger. This differs from the adjective extraño meaning “strange” or “weird.”

example.es: Un extraño llamó a la puerta.
example.en: A stranger knocked at the door.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Encantador describes a masculine singular person or thing. The feminine singular form is encantadora.
Encima places something in the upper position. It can stand alone when the reference point is understood; encima de names that reference point explicitly.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone invites a person to an event or treats them to food or a drink?
cards.answerEn: Use invitar for the invitation, identify the invited person, then use a before the event, activity, food, or drink.
cards.noteEn: Alguien means the person invited and algo means what they are invited to; they are placeholders, not words that must appear literally. A name often has a before it: invito a Marta. An object pronoun can replace the person: te invito. The second a introduces the invitation or treat.

example.en: I will treat you to a coffee.

cards.noteEn: Invitado is the completed-action form of invitar, “to invite.” With a person and a before a drink or meal, invitar can also mean to treat that person or buy it for them.

example.es: Te he invitado a un café.
example.en: I have treated you to a coffee.

cards.answerEn: to; for (introducing what someone is invited to)
cards.noteEn: After invitar and the invited person, a introduces the event, activity, food, or drink being offered.
Copa can name a stemmed glass or the alcoholic drink served in one. Invitar a una copa commonly means to buy someone a drink.

example.es: Tomaron una copa después del trabajo.
example.en: They had a drink after work.

cards.noteEn: Camarero can refer to a man serving customers in a restaurant or bar. Camarera is the feminine form.
A margarita is a cocktail commonly made with tequila, citrus juice, and orange liqueur. The same Spanish word also means “daisies,” but the bar context selects the drink meaning.

example.es: Pidieron dos margaritas en el bar.
example.en: They ordered two margaritas at the bar.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a container or place is full all the way to the top?
cards.answerEn: Use hasta arriba to mean filled to the top or completely full.
cards.noteEn: Hasta gives the endpoint and arriba supplies the upper limit. With a container it can be literal; with a place such as a bus or bar, it can also mean packed or completely full.

example.es: La caja está llena hasta arriba.
example.en: The box is full to the top.
